strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: extending HJB-based continuous-time RL from single-agent to multi-agent (CT-MARL) settings using PINNs.

The proposed Value Gradient Iteration (VGI) module is a reasonable and interesting mechanism to improve gradient fidelity in PINN-based value learning without requiring ground-truth gradient supervision, addressing a known PINN failure mode (poor gradient backpropagation from sparse boundary conditions).

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark families (continuous-time MPE, continuous-time multi-agent MuJoCo, and a custom coupled-oscillator environment with analytical LQR ground truth for interpretable validation).
Good set of ablations: VGI on/off, activation function choice, loss-term weighting, and robustness to varying time intervals, which help build a coherent story supporting design choices.

The didactic oscillator experiment with closed-form LQR ground truth is a nice touch, providing interpretable visual/quantitative evidence (Fig. 1, 3, 9) that VGI meaningfully improves value/gradient accuracy over the no-VGI ablation.
Provides theoretical scaffolding (HJB derivation, advantage definition, policy improvement, VGI contraction) which, while not airtight, shows the authors attempted to ground the method formally.
weaknesses: Baselines are weak and outdated for a top-tier venue: DPI and IPI both originate from a single 2021 single-agent paper (Lee & Sutton) and CT-MBRL (ODE) is also a single-agent method; the manuscript does not clearly explain how these were extended/adapted to the CTDE multi-agent setting, raising concerns about baseline implementation fidelity and fairness of comparison.

No comparison against standard, strong discrete-time MARL baselines (e.g., MADDPG, MAPPO, QMIX) across the main benchmark suite; MADDPG only appears in a single robustness plot (Fig. 8), which undercuts the claim that CT-MARL 'consistently outperforms' relevant alternatives.
HJB-PPO [27], a directly relevant PINN+RL baseline discussed extensively in Related Work, is never empirically compared against, despite being closely related prior art.

Some theoretical results are loosely derived: Lemma 3.3's proof assumes an exact greedy policy-improvement argmax at each step, which is inconsistent with the lemma's stated setting of 'one gradient step with sufficiently small step size'; several HJB derivations rely on informal Taylor expansions with approximate equalities rather than rigorous error bounds.

Theorem 3.4's contraction argument is a fairly standard/simple linear-operator contraction result contingent on the time step being sufficiently small; its practical implications for training stability at the actual (non-infinitesimal) step sizes used in experiments are not clearly established.

Novelty relative to prior differential-game value-gradient work (Zhang et al., refs 50 and 51) is incremental; the core idea of tying value learning to gradient learning for PINN-based HJB solving is already established, and VGI's contribution mainly replaces supervised ground-truth gradients with a bootstrapped self-consistent target.

Reliance on learned dynamics and reward models to compute the VGI target introduces compounding approximation errors that are not directly ablated or analyzed (e.g., sensitivity to model quality/error).

No real-world or physically realistic high-dimensional multi-agent task; MuJoCo/MPE variants are synthetic proxies for continuous-time interaction and the significance of results to genuinely high-frequency or irregular real-world control is not demonstrated.
Terminology inconsistency between the paper's framing as a CT-MARL framework and the introduced method name VIP may create confusion; presentation could be tightened.
Limited scope acknowledged by authors (cooperative-only, no competitive or general-sum CT-MARL), which somewhat narrows the practical significance of the contribution for broader MARL research.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: extending continuous-time RL (HJB/PINN-based) methods to the multi-agent setting, which prior CTRL literature has largely ignored.

The Value Gradient Iteration (VGI) module is a reasonable idea for improving gradient fidelity in PINN-based value learning, and the paper provides a convergence argument (contraction mapping) for the idealized iteration.

The paper includes a reasonably thorough set of ablations (VGI on/off, activation function choice, loss-term weighting, time-discretization robustness) and a clean didactic coupled-oscillator example with an analytical LQR ground truth for interpretable validation.
Two continuous-time benchmark suites (MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo) are constructed, providing some infrastructure that could be useful to the community.
weaknesses: Weak and dated baselines: the empirical comparisons are only against DPI/IPI (Lee & Sutton, 2021) and CT-MBRL/ODE (Yildiz et al., 2021), all single-agent CTRL methods naïvely extended to multi-agent. The paper explicitly cites more relevant and more recent CTRL-PINN works (e.g., HJB-PPO [27], Shilova et al. [34]) as closely related but never compares against them, even in adapted multi-agent form.

No strong discrete-time MARL baseline (e.g., MAPPO, MADDPG, QMIX) is evaluated on the main MPE/MuJoCo benchmarks -- DT-MARL comparison is confined to the small toy oscillator example (Fig. 1, Fig. 8), which is insufficient to support the paper's central motivating claim that CT-MARL is needed for realistic high-dimensional tasks.

The convergence guarantee (Theorem 3.4) is stated for an idealized affine contraction with a fixed, exact Jacobian and small Δt, but in practice the method uses *learned* dynamics/reward models (fψ, rϕ) with approximation error; no analysis connects the idealized contraction result to the actual algorithm's behavior with model/network error.

Proof of Lemma 3.3 (policy improvement) is informal/questionable: it assumes an unspecified invariant "goal state function," the step-size δt is not rigorously taken to zero within a stochastic/continuous control framework, and the argument largely mirrors discrete-time policy improvement without addressing continuous-time subtleties.

All quantitative results are presented only as reward curves with overlapping shaded regions (no tables, no numerical significance tests), making it difficult to judge whether reported improvements are statistically meaningful, especially given the high variance visible in Fig. 2 and Fig. 4.

The "continuous-time" benchmarks are constructed by simply randomizing Δt within a bounded range for standard MPE/MuJoCo tasks, which is a fairly superficial notion of continuous-time/irregular decision-making rather than a benchmark reflecting genuinely irregular or high-frequency real-world dynamics.

No discussion of computational overhead: the method trains a value network, dynamics model, reward model, and per-agent policy networks simultaneously with four loss terms, which likely incurs substantial extra cost relative to baselines, yet no wall-clock or sample-efficiency comparison is provided.

The claimed advantage of PINNs in mitigating the curse of dimensionality is not empirically substantiated at genuinely high dimensions -- the MuJoCo tasks involve only a handful of low-dimensional agents (e.g., 2 or 4 legs), not a demonstration of scaling to many agents/high state dimension.

The anchor (TD-style) loss added on top of the PDE residual loss makes the "pure HJB/PINN" framing somewhat inconsistent with standard actor-critic bootstrapping, diluting the claimed novelty of the value-iteration-via-PINN framing.

The method is restricted to cooperative settings with a shared centralized value function; this is acknowledged as a limitation but substantially narrows the claimed significance for general multi-agent RL.

Minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., typo "chllenges", inconsistent inline citation duplication such as [8] and [9] pointing to the same Doya reference) suggest the manuscript could benefit from more careful proofreading.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: extending continuous-time RL (HJB-based value learning) to the multi-agent setting, which is a reasonable and timely gap to fill.

The proposed Value Gradient Iteration (VGI) module is a sensible mechanism to reduce the noisy/biased gradients that standard PINN training produces, and the paper provides supporting theory (contraction mapping argument) for its convergence.
The paper builds new continuous-time variants of MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo benchmarks with variable time-step sampling, which could be a useful resource for the community if released.
Reasonably thorough empirical ablations: VGI on/off, activation function choice (Tanh vs ReLU), loss-term weighting, and robustness to varying time intervals.
The didactic coupled-oscillator environment with an analytical LQR solution provides an interpretable sanity check for value/gradient accuracy that many CTRL papers lack.
Clear presentation of the overall pipeline (critic loss combining HJB residual, terminal, anchor, and VGI losses) and an explicit training algorithm in the appendix aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivations are somewhat informal: Lemma 3.1's proof relies on loose Taylor-expansion approximations (e.g., treating T−Δt ≈ T, and approximate equalities marked with '≈') rather than a rigorous viscosity-solution argument, which weakens the claimed theoretical rigor for a paper that leans heavily on HJB theory.

Lemma 3.2 (instantaneous advantage) essentially restates the HJB residual as an 'advantage' via a first-order Taylor expansion; the conceptual novelty of this result is limited, and Lemma 3.3's 'policy improvement' proof glosses over technical details (e.g., what 'goal state function stays invariant' means, handling of continuous time indices) making it feel more heuristic than a formal guarantee.

Baseline comparison is narrow: aside from one comparison against MADDPG in the toy oscillator task, the main MPE/MuJoCo experiments only compare against three CTRL baselines (DPI, IPI, ODE), all adapted to the multi-agent setting by the authors themselves; there is no comparison against stronger discrete-time MARL methods (e.g., MAPPO, QMIX) under matched high-frequency settings, which would better substantiate the CTRL-vs-DTRL claims made in the introduction.

The core technical novelty (aligning value learning with a bootstrapped value-gradient target) closely mirrors ideas from prior work on value-gradient consistency in differential games (ref. [51]); the paper's contribution is largely in extending/combining this idea to the multi-agent PINN critic setting, which is a comparatively incremental step.

The VGI module requires auxiliary learned dynamics and reward models (fψ, rϕ); the paper does not analyze how sensitive the overall method is to errors in these learned models, nor does it report additional computational overhead (training time, sample complexity) relative to baselines, despite PINN-based training typically being expensive.

Results are based on only 5 seeds with wide variance bands in several MuJoCo tasks (e.g., Cheetah, Swimmer), and no statistical significance testing is reported, making some of the performance gaps difficult to assess as robust.

Scalability claims are not strongly tested: the multi-agent settings used (2-6 agents in MPE/MuJoCo) are still relatively small, so it's unclear how well the centralized PINN-based value function would scale to substantially larger numbers of agents, despite the paper motivating the work partly around curse-of-dimensionality concerns.
The limitation of the work to purely cooperative tasks is acknowledged but somewhat narrows the significance of the contribution relative to the broader claim of solving 'CT-MARL problems.'

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: extending continuous-time RL (HJB/PINN-based value learning) to the multi-agent cooperative setting, which prior CTRL work has largely ignored.

The Value Gradient Iteration (VGI) module is a sensible mechanism for improving gradient accuracy beyond what PDE residual losses alone provide, and the paper supports it with a fixed-point/contraction argument (Theorem 3.4) as well as clear empirical ablations (Fig. 3, 6, 10) showing improved value/gradient fidelity when VGI is included.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning continuous-time MPE, continuous-time multi-agent MuJoCo (up to 113 state dims, 6 agents), and a fully interpretable didactic coupled-oscillator task with an analytical LQR ground truth for validating value and gradient accuracy.

Multiple relevant ablations are provided: VGI on/off, activation function choice (Tanh vs ReLU), loss-term weighting, robustness to stochastic dynamics noise, sensitivity to the discretization step ∆t, and comparison against both CTRL and DTRL baselines (MADDPG, MATD3, MAPPO).

Formal derivations (HJB PDE, instantaneous advantage, policy improvement, VGI convergence) are provided with proofs in the appendix, giving the method some theoretical grounding beyond a purely heuristic construction.
weaknesses: It is unclear how single-agent CTRL baselines (DPI, IPI, ODE, HJBPPO) were adapted to the multi-agent setting — this is a critical methodological detail left unspecified, raising concern that these may be weak or improperly adapted (e.g., naive centralization) comparisons rather than strong, fairly-tuned baselines.

Several of the theoretical results (Lemma 3.1 HJB derivation, Lemma 3.2 instantaneous advantage) are essentially standard first-order Taylor/Bellman expansions already well known in continuous-time control literature, limiting the technical novelty of the theory section; the VGI idea itself closely resembles costate/adjoint gradient propagation used in Pontryagin-based differential game value approximation (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024a;b), and the paper does not clearly delineate its novelty relative to this closely related line of work.

The VGI convergence guarantee (Theorem 3.4) relies on a first-order Euler linearization and a contraction condition that only holds for sufficiently small ∆t; this restrictive requirement is corroborated by the paper's own sensitivity analysis (Appendix C.4), which shows sharp performance degradation once ∆t exceeds a modest threshold, somewhat undercutting the claimed robustness to irregular/large time intervals.

The anchor loss reintroduces a TD-style bootstrapped one-step-return target computed via discretized rollouts, which is in tension with the paper's core narrative of avoiding time-discretization; the practical algorithm still depends on ∆t-based rollouts for training rather than being purely continuous.

No wall-clock time, sample efficiency, or computational cost comparison is provided despite PINN-based training (auto-diff of PDE residuals, dynamics/reward model fitting, VGI targets) being generally far more expensive than standard model-free RL — this omission makes it hard to assess the practical scalability claims.

Reported results lack statistical significance testing; although 5 seeds are used, variance bands in several figures (e.g., VIP vs. VIP w/o VGI in some MuJoCo tasks) appear to overlap substantially, weakening the strength of the 'consistently outperforms' claim.

The continuous-time benchmark modifications (random ∆t sampling ranges, reward rescaling) are somewhat ad hoc and not rigorously justified or validated as faithful continuous-time analogues of the original discrete benchmarks.

Scope is limited to cooperative, deterministic, single-agent-style advantage decomposition; extension to stochastic dynamics or competitive/mixed settings is left entirely to future work, and the noise-robustness experiment (Appendix C.3) shows substantial performance degradation under even moderate stochastic perturbation, suggesting limited real-world applicability.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored problem: extending continuous-time RL/HJB-based value learning via PINNs to the cooperative multi-agent setting (CTDE), which has seen little prior work compared to single-agent CTRL.
The Value Gradient Iteration (VGI) module is a reasonable and intuitively motivated mechanism to improve the accuracy of value gradients, which matter directly for HJB-residual-based policy updates.

Fairly broad empirical evaluation spanning a didactic LQR-verifiable coupled-oscillator task, continuous-time MPE, and continuous-time multi-agent MuJoCo, with ablations on VGI, activation function choice, and loss-term weighting.

Inclusion of an analytically solvable linear-quadratic didactic environment allows direct comparison of learned value/gradient surfaces against ground truth, which is a nice sanity-check design choice.
Comparisons against both continuous-time baselines (ODE, DPI, IPI, HJBPPO) and discrete-time MARL baselines (MADDPG, MATD3, MAPPO) to contextualize the benefit of the continuous-time formulation.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions are not rigorous: Lemma 3.3's 'proof' is an informal telescoping-sum sketch that glosses over how one-step Q-improvement under function approximation propagates to the infinite-horizon return, and it invokes an expectation inequality without justification; this undermines the claimed policy-improvement guarantee.

Theorem 3.4's contraction result relies on a first-order Euler linearization and a 'sufficiently small Δt' assumption, which is a fairly weak/local guarantee; this is also empirically confirmed in Appendix C.4, where performance degrades sharply once Δt leaves a narrow regime, limiting the practical scope of the claimed robustness to irregular sampling.

VGI is conceptually close to standard semi-gradient/Bellman-style bootstrapping applied to the gradient instead of the value, combined with an already-used anchor/TD loss and PDE residual loss (as in HJBPPO and other PINN-RL works); the core novelty over existing single-agent PINN+RL frameworks (e.g., HJBPPO, Shilova et al.) appears incremental, mainly extending these to the multi-agent CTDE setting.

The method assumes fully deterministic dynamics; Appendix C.3 shows substantial performance degradation even under moderate stochastic noise, which is a major limitation given most realistic multi-agent systems are stochastic, undercutting claims of broad applicability.

Scale of experiments is modest (up to six agents, 113 state dimensions) for a paper emphasizing 'scaling to complex cooperative multi-agent dynamics'; no study of how performance/training cost scales with agent count or state dimension beyond this range.

The approach requires jointly training a value network, N policy networks, plus separate dynamics and reward models, substantially increasing computational and sample complexity versus baselines; no runtime/sample-efficiency comparison is provided to contextualize this overhead.

Comparisons to discrete-time MARL baselines (MADDPG/MATD3/MAPPO) trained/evaluated on variable-Δt rollouts largely reconfirm an already well-known failure mode of fixed-step Bellman methods under irregular sampling, rather than providing new insight; a more informative comparison would include DTRL methods explicitly adapted to variable Δt rather than only showing their expected degradation.

No comparison to any existing multi-agent/differential-game PINN value-approximation methods (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024a;b, cited as closely related), despite these being natural baselines for coupled value-gradient learning in multi-agent continuous-time settings.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: the paper references 'Code is available at this link' without an actual accessible link in the text, and environment/algorithmic details, while present in the appendix, leave some implementation specifics (e.g., exact network update schedules, model-based rollout procedure) underspecified.

Results are reported over only 5 seeds, with relatively wide and overlapping confidence bands in several plots (e.g., Fig. 2, Fig. 9), raising questions about the statistical significance of the reported performance gaps over baselines.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified and relatively underexplored gap: extending continuous-time RL (CTRL) via PINN-approximated HJB value functions to the cooperative multi-agent setting.

The proposed Value Gradient Iteration (VGI) module is a reasonable and novel idea for improving gradient accuracy of PINN-based critics, supported by a fixed-point/contraction convergence argument (Theorem 3.4).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark families (continuous-time MPE, continuous-time multi-agent MuJoCo, and a didactic coupled-oscillator task with closed-form LQR ground truth), allowing both qualitative and quantitative validation of value/gradient accuracy.
Good set of ablations: VGI on/off, activation function choice (Tanh vs ReLU), loss-term weighting, time-discretization sensitivity, and comparison to both CTRL and DTRL baselines.
The didactic LQR example with exact value/gradient ground truth is a nice, interpretable validation of the core claim that accurate value gradients matter.
Additional appendix experiments on noise robustness and ∆t sensitivity provide useful insight into the operating regime and limitations of the method.
Derivations/proofs for the HJB formulation, instantaneous advantage, and policy improvement are provided, giving some theoretical grounding to the method.
weaknesses: The contraction proof for VGI (Theorem 3.4) relies on treating the Jacobian ∇x f as effectively time-invariant along the trajectory to get a single matrix A; in practice xt, ut vary along the trajectory, so the argument is somewhat informal/hand-wavy and the global contraction claim is not rigorously justified over an entire trajectory of varying states/actions.

The claim of being essentially the first to tackle CT-MARL is undercut by very thin discussion of prior CT-MARL work (only two papers cited), making it hard to assess true novelty versus existing model-based continuous-time multi-agent value iteration methods (e.g., Jiang et al. 2023).

The policy update (Eq. 8) uses a single shared global advantage computed from the centralized critic for all agents' policy gradients; this does not address multi-agent credit assignment and is a fairly simplistic CTDE realization compared to more principled approaches (e.g., counterfactual baselines).

"Continuous-time" MPE/MuJoCo benchmarks are implemented via randomly sampled discretization step sizes rather than genuinely continuous simulation, which is a reasonable proxy but somewhat overstates the continuous-time nature of the experiments.

Only 5 random seeds are used, and the reported confidence bands in several MuJoCo tasks (e.g., Swimmer, HalfCheetah, Walker) show substantial overlap between VIP and baselines, raising questions about the statistical robustness of the claimed consistent improvements.

The VGI target (Eq. 10/12) depends on learned dynamics and reward models (fψ, rϕ); the compounding effect of their approximation errors on the gradient target is not analyzed, despite this being central to the proposed stability argument.

The approach is restricted to deterministic cooperative multi-agent systems; the appendix shows sharp performance degradation under even moderate stochastic noise, which limits applicability to many realistic multi-agent domains with inherent stochasticity.

No wall-clock time, computational overhead, or sample-efficiency-per-unit-compute comparisons are reported, which is important given the added complexity of PINN residual computation, dynamics/reward model learning, and VGI refinement relative to baselines.
